newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Fine wool leaves coarse wool in wake at NZ sales.
newsitem.headline: Fine wool leaves coarse wool in wake at NZ sales.

text.p: Farmers' fears that a big fall in the New Zealand dollar would fail to translate into significantly higher prices for coarse wools were borne out at the season's first sales in Christchurch and Napier on Thursday.
While the fine wool indicator jumped 101 cents to 1078 NZ cents/kg clean from the last sale on June 26, the strong segment indicator only rose 12 cents to 399.
The overall market indicator closed up 21 cents to 484 cents. The medium segment indicator was up 24 cents to 623 and the lamb segment up 30 cents to 474 cents.
Fine wool prices responded to higher prices seen in Australia and to the 10 percent depreciation of the New Zealand dollar from a peak in November, but demand for coarse wools was only modest.
New Zealand produces mostly coarse wools used mainly for carpets, furnishings and hank knitting yarn.
"The only ones to have gained the full extent of the devaluation, plus a little bit, would be the merinos," said Michael Dwyer of Wools International.
"The coarse wools are basically unchanged on the previous sales so they've fallen in hard currency terms."
"It's the coarse end of the clip that is causing anguish. That's the area where the market is soft. It doesn't look too heartening at this stage. It's a bit disappointing," he said.
Wrightson's regional wool manager in Napier Richard Wakeland said prices were lower than expected and the full effect of the lower exchange rate was not yet coming through.
Some 28 percent of the 4,178 tonnes on offer at the sales was passed in.
The offerings included 32 percent second shear, 25 percent crossbred fleece, 10 percent halfbred fleece, 11 percent crutchings, 7 percent second shear bellies and pieces and 2 percent merino fleece.

All wools were dearer against the June 26 sales -- merino by 7.5-10 percent, halfbred 26-27 micron by 5-7 percent, halfbred 28-33 micron by 3-4 percent, crossbred 38 micron and finer by 2.5-5 percent, crossbred 39 micron and stronger by 0-2 percent, second shear 2.5-10 percent and first lambs by 2-5 percent.
Main interest came from Western Europe, local mills and China with support from India and Pakistan.
The next sale will be at Christchurch on August 14.
